content.summary_of_the_paper: This paper studies label differential privacy, and proposes a novel PLE approach to mask the sensitive label while ensuring the utility of predictive model. The properties of classifier-consistent and ERM learnable of the predictive model are provided with theory. And the proposed methods behave well in experiments.
content.strength_and_weaknesses:
Strength:
The idea seems interesting and the paper is clear with no major typos.
The PLE model is trainable, and several carefully designed losses are provided to punish if the true label appears at the top or disappears in the top-k_1. 
A framework of the predictive model is designed with theory to force it can disambiguate the true label from the protective label distribution. 

Weakness:
In the "Label Enhancement'' of section 2, the authors mentioned the proposed PLE provides privacy guarantees..., however, no guarantees or discussions were found. It seems the quoted privacy comes from the random mechanism for label. Thus the level of privacy-preserving is unclear. It is better to provide a privacy analysis when it comes to DP.

Another one is about the accuracy comparison in Experiments. The results doesn't convince me because of the possibly inconsistent privacy budget. The budget of compared methods is calculated by theory while the proposed method is through tuning a hyperparameter \gamma.
content.clarity,_quality,_novelty_and_reproducib: Good:  The paper is well organized but the presentation has minor details that could be improved, and appears to be technically sound. The proofs appear to be correct, but I have not carefully checked the details.  The paper contributes some new ideas or represents incremental advances.
content.summary_of_the_review: This paper has done a good job, but I have some concerns as above. Can the authors fix the issues?

content.summary_of_the_paper: The paper proposes an approach for label distribution privacy which involves penalizing selecting the correct label while promoting top k accuracy and independence of top k labels. Some heuristics are then used when learning a classifier from the label differentially private data. Theoretical results are provided demonstrating the utility of the approach.
content.strength_and_weaknesses:
Strengths:
- The general idea proposed seems interesting
- The theoretical results appear rigorous

Weaknesses:
- The paper is very difficult to read in certain sections and certain parts of the setup are unclear
- The primary novel idea is not well described in the text - (3) on page 4
- The approach lacks a means for controlling the privacy level (not mentioned until late in the text)
content.clarity,_quality,_novelty_and_reproducib:
The theoretical results appear to be novel. It's somewhat unclear how much of the methodological contributions other than (3) are novel. 

Clarity, both in details of the approach as well as the text in general and discussion of background material, needs to be improved. Thorough proofreading is necessary.
content.summary_of_the_review: The paper presents an interesting idea for improving label differential privacy, but is difficult to read with many details unclear and the approach does not provide a means for controlling the privacy level.

content.summary_of_the_paper: The paper proposes a method for generating synthetic data that satisfies an informal notion of label privacy. It proves a theoretical optimality result and a PAC-style sample complexity result based on the "ambiguity" of the data distribution. It concludes by justifying the solution's privacy and accuracy through an empirical comparison to label DP baselines from the literature.
content.strength_and_weaknesses:
Strengths: I don't think there has been a truly convincing privacy story for label privacy. This paper perhaps deserves some credit for attempting to craft one.

Weaknesses: The paper's primary weakness is that it provides no real privacy guarantee. Despite the abstract and introduction's focus on label DP, the paper does not attempt to construct a label DP solution. Instead, it proposes a heuristic solution based on randomizing labels to produce synthetic data. The argument that this solution is "private" relies on experiments on CIFAR-10 and CIFAR-100 showing that the solution produces synthetic labels that match the true labels at roughly the same rate as baseline methods that actually satisfy label DP. By the paper's reasoning, since the proposed method has similar "accuracy of the response" as label DP methods, it has similar privacy guarantees. It is easy to see that this argument does not offer meaningful privacy. For example, a deterministic rule that simply shifts labels (1 -> 2, 2 -> 3, ..., c -> 1) will have 0% "accuracy of the response", and thus "perfect" privacy according to this notion, while essentially revealing all of the labels. It is therefore hard to take the paper's assertion that "accuracy of the response [is] a more accurate and intuitive indicator to measure the degree of privacy protection [than an eps-DP guarantee]" seriously.

Given the paper's essentially meaningless privacy guarantee, I do not see the value in its utility guarantees (and did not look at them closely).

As a general and lower-order comment, the paper is also hard to read. The grammar is often strange, indexing variables switch without warning (i indexes labels in Section 3.1, then data points in Section 3.2 [though it indexes the sums but doesn't appear in the summands, and this happens in Equation 11 too], then epochs in Algorithm 1), the number of "data augmentations" is variously referred to as m or \kappa, I don't know what the R in Theorem 1 is, etc.

Nonetheless, my negative impression of this paper is almost entirely driven by the weakness of its privacy guarantee.
content.clarity,_quality,_novelty_and_reproducib: See above; I think all are low.
content.summary_of_the_review: The paper proposes an algorithm satisfying a heuristic notion of privacy that it introduces and barely justifies beyond vague notions of intuition. As described above, it is easy to construct algorithms that obtain perfect privacy under this definition but are clearly qualitatively not private. It is hard for me to see the value of this kind of privacy guarantee, so the paper's contribution seems very weak.

content.title: Protective Label Enhancement for Label Privacy
content.abstract: Much sensitive data is gathered from the individual device for commercial value without effective safeguards over the past decade, which would bring on serious privacy leakage. Here we review the label differential privacy (label DP), which means that only the labels are sensitive. The generated private labels of previous methods do not consider the label confidence corresponding to the feature and multiple sampling could be employed to identify the true labels. In the paper, a novel approach called Protective Label Enhancement (PLE) is proposed to mask the true label in the label distribution while ensuring that the protective label distribution is utility for training an effective predictive model on the server. Specifically, when we generate the label distribution, the true label is mixed up by choosing several random labels and the true label will be punished when it is at the top of the label distribution. Meanwhile, if the true label almost vanishes, it will be compensated to keep the statistical effectiveness. Furthermore, we provide the corresponding theoretical guarantee that the predictive model is classifier-consistent and that learning with the protective label distribution is ERM learnable. Finally, experimental results clearly validate the effectiveness of the proposed approach for solving the label DP problem.
